title: Oxytocin
subtitle: The positive and negative effects of the chemical known as the ‘love hormone’
overallInstruction: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.
overallInstructionZh: 你应该用大约20分钟完成第14–26题，这些题目基于下面的阅读文章2。

bodyParagraphs.label: A
sentences: Oxytocin is a chemical, a hormone produced in the pituitary gland in the brain.
It was through various studies focusing on animals that scientists first became aware of the influence of oxytocin.
They discovered that it helps reinforce the bonds between prairie voles, which mate for life, and triggers the motherly behaviour that sheep show towards their newborn lambs.
It is also released by women in childbirth, strengthening the attachment between mother and baby.
Few chemicals have as positive a reputation as oxytocin, which is sometimes referred to as the ‘love hormone’.
One sniff of it can, it is claimed, make a person more trusting, empathetic, generous and cooperative.
It is time, however, to revise this wholly optimistic view.
A new wave of studies has shown that its effects vary greatly depending on the person and the circumstances, and it can impact on our social interactions for worse as well as for better.

bodyParagraphs.label: B
sentences: Oxytocin’s role in human behaviour first emerged in 2005.

In a groundbreaking experiment, Markus Heinrichs and his colleagues at the University of Freiburg, Germany, asked volunteers to do an activity in which they could invest money with an anonymous person who was not guaranteed to be honest.
The team found that participants who had sniffed oxytocin via a nasal spray beforehand invested more money than those who received a placebo instead.
The study was the start of research into the effects of oxytocin on human interactions.
‘For eight years, it was quite a lonesome field,’ Heinrichs recalls.
‘Now, everyone is interested.’
These follow-up studies have shown that after a sniff of the hormone, people become more charitable, better at reading emotions on others’ faces and at communicating constructively in arguments.
Together, the results fuelled the view that oxytocin universally enhanced the positive aspects of our social nature.

bodyParagraphs.label: C
sentences: Then, after a few years, contrasting findings began to emerge.

Simone Shamay-Tsoory at the University of Haifa, Israel, found that when volunteers played a competitive game, those who inhaled the hormone showed more pleasure when they beat other players, and felt more envy when others won.
What’s more, administering oxytocin also has sharply contrasting outcomes depending on a person’s disposition.
Jennifer Bartz from Mount Sinai School of Medicine, New York, found that it improves people’s ability to read emotions, but only if they are not very socially adept to begin with.
Her research also shows that oxytocin in fact reduces cooperation in subjects who are particularly anxious or sensitive to rejection.

bodyParagraphs.label: D
sentences: Another discovery is that oxytocin’s effects vary depending on who we are interacting with.

Studies conducted by Carolyn DeClerck of the University of Antwerp, Belgium, revealed that people who had received a dose of oxytocin actually became less cooperative when dealing with complete strangers.

Meanwhile, Carsten De Dreu at the University of Amsterdam in the Netherlands discovered that volunteers given oxytocin showed favouritism: Dutch men became quicker to associate positive words with Dutch names than with foreign ones, for example.
According to De Dreu, oxytocin drives people to care for those in their social circles and defend them from outside dangers.
So, it appears that oxytocin strengthens biases, rather than promoting general goodwill, as was previously thought.

bodyParagraphs.label: E
sentences: There were signs of these subtleties from the start.
Bartz has recently shown that in almost half of the existing research results, oxytocin influenced only certain individuals or in certain circumstances.
Where once researchers took no notice of such findings, now a more nuanced understanding of oxytocin’s effects is propelling investigations down new lines.
To Bartz, the key to understanding what the hormone does lies in pinpointing its core function rather than in cataloguing its seemingly endless effects.
There are several hypotheses which are not mutually exclusive.
Oxytocin could help to reduce anxiety and fear.
Or it could simply motivate people to seek out social connections.

She believes that oxytocin acts as a chemical spotlight that shines on social cues – a shift in posture, a flicker of the eyes, a dip in the voice – making people more attuned to their social environment.
This would explain why it makes us more likely to look others in the eye and improves our ability to identify emotions.
But it could also make things worse for people who are overly sensitive or prone to interpreting social cues in the worst light.

bodyParagraphs.label: F
sentences: Perhaps we should not be surprised that the oxytocin story has become more perplexing.
The hormone is found in everything from octopuses to sheep, and its evolutionary roots stretch back half a billion years.
‘It’s a very simple and ancient molecule that has been co-opted for many different functions,’ says Sue Carter at the University of Illinois, Chicago, USA.
‘It affects primitive parts of the brain like the amygdala, so it’s going to have many effects on just about everything.’
Bartz agrees.

‘Oxytocin probably does some very basic things, but once you add our higher-order thinking and social situations, these basic processes could manifest in different ways depending on individual differences and context.’

questions.reasoning: a lonesome field 表示这一研究领域当时参与者少，对应 little scientific attention。
questions.distractors: F谈历史悠久而非科学关注度；E说忽略某些研究发现，含义不同。

questions.stem: reference to people ignoring certain aspects of their research data

questions.evidence: Where once researchers took no notice of such findings, now a more nuanced understanding of oxytocin’s effects is propelling investigations down new lines.
questions.reasoning: took no notice of such findings 直接同义替换 ignoring certain aspects of research data。
questions.distractors: B是领域受冷落；题干则是研究者忽略已经出现的结果。

questions.stem: People are more trusting when affected by oxytocin.
questions.stemZh: 人们受催产素影响时会更加信任他人。
questions.evidence: The team found that participants who had sniffed oxytocin via a nasal spray beforehand invested more money than those who received a placebo instead.
questions.reasoning: 愿意向无法保证诚实的匿名对象投入更多钱，体现 more trusting；该实验由 Heinrichs 团队完成。
questions.distractors: B研究竞争中的嫉妒；C研究个体差异；D研究陌生人合作；E研究内群体偏爱；F解释进化与脑机制。

questions.stem: Oxytocin increases people’s feelings of jealousy.
questions.stemZh: 催产素增强人的嫉妒感。
questions.evidence: Simone Shamay-Tsoory ... found that ... those who inhaled the hormone ... felt more envy when others won.
questions.reasoning: jealousy 与原文 envy 同义，研究者是 Simone Shamay-Tsoory。
questions.distractors: 其余研究者的发现分别涉及信任、识别情绪、陌生人合作、偏爱和机制。

questions.stem: The effect of oxytocin varies from one type of person to another.
questions.stemZh: 催产素的作用因人而异。
questions.evidence: Jennifer Bartz ... found that it improves people’s ability to read emotions, but only if they are not very socially adept to begin with.
questions.reasoning: only if 限定某一类人，说明作用随人的类型而变化。
questions.distractors: D、E考查互动对象或群体偏向，不是受试者本人的类型差异。

questions.stem: The earliest findings about oxytocin and bonding came from research involving ________.
questions.stemZh: 关于催产素与情感联结的最早发现来自涉及________的研究。
questions.evidence: It was through various studies focusing on animals that scientists first became aware of the influence of oxytocin.
questions.reasoning: research involving 对应 studies focusing on；答案 animals 为原文一个词。
questions.distractors: prairie voles 和 sheep 是具体例子，但概括空需要上位词 animals。

questions.stem: It was also discovered that humans produce oxytocin during ________.
questions.stemZh: 研究还发现，人类在________期间会产生催产素。

questions.reasoning: produce oxytocin 对应 is released；during 对应 in，填 childbirth。
questions.distractors: attachment 是释放后的作用，不是发生时间。

questions.stem: An experiment in 2005, in which participants were given either oxytocin or a ________, reinforced the belief that the hormone had a positive effect.
questions.stemZh: 2005年的实验给参与者使用催产素或________，强化了该激素有积极作用的看法。
questions.evidence: The team found that participants who had sniffed oxytocin via a nasal spray beforehand invested more money than those who received a placebo instead.
questions.reasoning: either oxytocin or 与原文 oxytocin 组和 placebo 对照组对应。
questions.distractors: spray 是给药方式；placebo 才是与 oxytocin 对照的物质。

questions.stem: A study at the University of Haifa where participants took part in a ________, revealed the negative emotions which oxytocin can trigger.
questions.stemZh: 海法大学的研究让参与者参加一场________，揭示了催产素可能触发的负面情绪。
questions.evidence: Simone Shamay-Tsoory at the University of Haifa, Israel, found that when volunteers played a competitive game ... felt more envy when others won.
questions.reasoning: took part in 对应 played；冠词 a 后填单数名词 game。
questions.distractors: competitive 虽在原文出现，但它是形容词，无法单独充当 a 后的中心名词。

questions.stem: A study at the University of Antwerp showed people’s lack of willingness to help ________ while under the influence of oxytocin.
questions.stemZh: 安特卫普大学的研究显示，人在催产素影响下不愿帮助________。
questions.evidence: Studies conducted by Carolyn DeClerck of the University of Antwerp, Belgium, revealed that people who had received a dose of oxytocin actually became less cooperative when dealing with complete strangers.
questions.reasoning: lack of willingness to help 对应 less cooperative；对象为 strangers。
questions.distractors: complete 是修饰词；只能填一词且语义中心是 strangers。

questions.stem: People who have been given oxytocin consider ________ that are familiar to them in their own country to have more positive associations than those from other cultures.
questions.stemZh: 使用催产素的人认为本国熟悉的________比其他文化中的对应事物有更积极的联想。
questions.evidence: Dutch men became quicker to associate positive words with Dutch names than with foreign ones, for example.
questions.reasoning: familiar in their own country 对应 Dutch；those from other cultures 对应 foreign ones，比较对象是 names。
questions.distractors: words 是被联想到的 positive 内容；实际被比较的是 Dutch names 与 foreign ones。
